title: 'No Reason to Shy Away': Germany's Merz Pushes Back on Trump's NATO Spending Criticism
summary: A war of words over wallets is heating up between Washington and Berlin. President Donald Trump this week renewed his long-standing criticism of NATO allies, singling out Germany's defense spending as 'MUCH LOWER' than the U.S. and calling the imbalance 'Ridiculous!' But German Chancellor Friedrich Merz fired back on Friday, insisting his country is making unprecedented efforts to bolster its military. 'This is the greatest effort we have ever made to strengthen our defense capabilities,' Merz told reporters. 'In this respect, we have no reason to shy away from anyone.' The clash comes just days before NATO leaders convene in Ankara, Turkey, for a summit likely to be dominated by transatlantic tensions. At the heart of the dispute is a 2025 agreement, pushed by Trump, that commits NATO members to spend 3.5% of their gross domestic product on core defense by 2035—a sharp increase from the previous 2% benchmark. Merz claims Germany is on track to meet that target as early as 2029, six years ahead of schedule. He noted that Germany, as the European Union's largest member state, bears a special responsibility within Europe. The spending spat is just one flashpoint in a deeply strained relationship. Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of acquiring Greenland, an autonomous Danish territory—and Denmark is a NATO ally. More recently, the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran has driven a wedge between Washington and European capitals. Trump launched the conflict without consulting allies, who have since grappled with the fallout, including the closure of the strategic Strait of Hormuz. Merz further roiled the White House in April by saying the U.S. had been 'humiliated' by Iran. Trump retaliated by announcing the withdrawal of 5,000 American troops stationed in Germany. Despite the friction, Merz struck a diplomatic tone. 'We will state this, with all due modesty,' he said, emphasizing Germany's commitment to the alliance. Whether that will satisfy Trump—who has long argued Europe freeloads on American military might—remains to be seen.
why_it_matters: This dispute shows how even close allies can clash over money and military power, and it raises questions about how the world’s security will be shared in a future where the U.S. may expect Europe to do much more on its own.

keywords.explanation: To bolster means to strengthen or support something, like a military force.
Something unprecedented has never happened before or is far beyond what is normal.
Transatlantic tensions are strains in the relationship between countries on opposite sides of the Atlantic Ocean, especially the US and Europe.
A benchmark is a standard or reference point against which things can be measured or compared.
To retaliate means to do something harmful back to someone because they did something harmful to you first.
Freeloads means getting benefits or protection without paying a fair share of the costs.

background_read: NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization) is a military alliance of 31 countries in North America and Europe that promises to defend each other if one of them is attacked.
Friedrich Merz, the new German Chancellor, leads the center-right CDU party and took office after elections in a period of shifting European politics.

For years, U.S. presidents have pushed NATO allies to spend more on defense; in 2014, during the Obama administration, NATO set a guideline for members to spend 2% of GDP on defense by 2024, and many countries, including Germany, consistently missed that mark.
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which a large portion of the world’s oil and goods pass—making it a critical chokepoint in any conflict involving Iran.

Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark, not an independent country, and Trump’s idea of acquiring it raised alarms in Copenhagen and among other NATO allies who saw it as an attack on Danish sovereignty.

perspectives.description: Germany’s plan to reach the 3.5% target early signals a real commitment to shared defense, which could make NATO stronger and more balanced in the long run.

Trump’s confrontational style—linking troop withdrawals to a political disagreement—risks weakening trust among allies and could push Europe to build its own military structures outside NATO, fracturing the alliance.

The friction reflects deeper power shifts: the U.S. wants to focus more on Asia and the Middle East, so it pressures Europe to take ownership of its own security. This isn’t just about money—it’s about a changing world order.

If the tension continues, the upcoming Ankara summit may lead to compromises, but it could also accelerate European defense integration, possibly laying foundations for a more independent EU military.
